Sikhism: Practices

  1. Mission 1Why does a Sikh place of worship have a kitchen, a throne and a flag you can see from far away?

Mission 1

Mission 1: Why does a Sikh place of worship have a kitchen, a throne and a flag you can see from far away?

Make a guess: Why does a Sikh place of worship have a kitchen, a throne and a flag you can see from far away?

Mission 1

The door of the Guru

  • Gurdwara means "door (or gateway) of the Guru".
  • Any building where the Guru Granth Sahib is installed with honour is a gurdwara.
  • Guru Nanak's community at Kartarpur met in a dharamsal (place of faith); later such places came to be called gurdwaras.
  • Three purposes: to house the Guru; to gather the sangat (community); to serve anyone who comes.
Mission 1

Outside: flag and doors

  • Nishan Sahib: a tall flagpole wrapped in cloth, with a triangular saffron (or blue) flag bearing the Khanda symbol.
  • It tells travellers: here is a gurdwara, with shelter, food and welcome for all.
  • The flag and its cloth are renewed every year at Vaisakhi.
  • Four doors: the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar has doors on all four sides.
  • Meaning: people from every direction, of every caste and every faith, are welcome.
  • Most local gurdwaras keep the idea by opening their doors to all, even if the building has one entrance.
  • On entering: shoes off, head covered, hands washed; no tobacco or alcohol.
Mission 1

The prayer hall

  • The main hall is the diwan hall (court); the Guru Granth Sahib is its sovereign.
  • Takht: the raised throne on which the Guru Granth Sahib rests, higher than everyone in the room.
  • Palki: the ornate canopied structure, like a royal carriage, around the takht.
  • Manji sahib: the small stand on which the scripture lies, with cushions and cloths (rumalas).
  • Chanani: the canopy above it, a sign of honour.
  • Chaur: the whisk waved over the scripture by the reader or a sewadar, as over a monarch.
  • Everyone sits on the floor at the same level: no seats of honour. Often men and women sit on different sides, by custom.
  • No statues and no pictures to bow to: Sikhs bow (matha tekna) only to the Guru Granth Sahib, and may leave an offering.
Mission 1

Sach khand and the langar hall

  • Sach khand ("realm of truth"): the room where the Guru Granth Sahib is laid to rest each night (sukhasan) and brought out at dawn (prakash).
  • Its name links to the highest stage of the soul's journey to God.
  • Langar hall: a kitchen and dining hall where a free meal is served to anyone.
  • Volunteers cook, serve and wash up. People sit in rows on the floor (pangat), side by side.
  • Langar as an expression of sewa: a later mission.
Quick check
?A visitor notices that during the service someone gently waves a whisk over the Guru Granth Sahib. What is it called, and why is it used?
Mission 1

What happens there: the gurdwara's role

  • Worship: morning and evening prayers; kirtan (hymns sung with harmonium and tabla); katha (talks); Ardas (standing prayer); the day's hukamnama.
  • Karah prashad: a sweet offering (flour, sugar, ghee) given to everyone equally at the end.
  • Ceremonies: naming, Amrit initiation, weddings (Anand Karaj), funeral prayers, Akhand Paths.
  • Learning: Punjabi and Gurmukhi classes, kirtan lessons, Sikh history, gatka (martial art).
  • Community: langar every day, help for elderly and new arrivals, food banks, shelter in emergencies.
  • In Britain many gurdwaras hold the main gathering on Sunday, when most people are free; daily prayers continue all week.
  • Role: the gurdwara is where Sikhs meet the Guru and the sangat, and practise sewa.
Quick check
?Why is karah prashad given to everyone in the gurdwara, in the same way?
Mission 1

Bhatra and Ramgarhia gurdwaras in Britain

  • Many British towns have more than one gurdwara. Some are linked to communities with their own history.
  • Bhatra Sikhs: among the earliest Sikhs to settle in Britain (from the 1920s and 1930s), many working as door-to-door traders. Their community traces its faith back to Guru Nanak's time.
  • Ramgarhia Sikhs: a community of skilled craftsmen (carpenters, builders, engineers), named after the 18th-century Sikh leader Jassa Singh Ramgarhia. Many came to Britain from East Africa in the 1960s–70s.
  • Social and community roles: support for newcomers, a place to keep language, customs and family networks; welfare, weddings and community events.
  • Places of worship: the same Guru Granth Sahib, prayers, kirtan and langar as any gurdwara; open to all.
  • A tension: Sikh teaching rejects caste. Some Sikhs say community-named gurdwaras keep caste divisions alive. Their members reply that the names record history and community, not rank, and that all are welcome.
Mission 1Diversity

How important is the gurdwara today?

  • Essential: the Guru Granth Sahib is present there, and Sikhs need the sangat to grow spiritually. Many visit daily.
  • Helpful, not essential: God is everywhere; nam japna and Nitnem happen at home and at work. Some Sikhs visit mainly on Sundays and festivals.
  • Keep features as they are: e.g. langar eaten sitting on the floor, as a sign of equality; services in Punjabi.
  • Adapt features: e.g. chairs for elderly or disabled people; English translations on screens for young Sikhs and visitors.
  • Sikhs disagree on how far adaptation should go; all keep the Guru Granth Sahib at the centre.
Mission 1Evaluate

"The gurdwara is the most important part of Sikh life."

  • Reasons for: the Guru Granth Sahib is there; worship with the sangat; langar and sewa happen there; ceremonies that mark life's stages take place there.
  • Reasons against: the Gurus taught that God is everywhere; remembering God's Name in daily life (GGS 305) matters more than a building. Honest work and sharing happen at home and at work. Sikhs without a gurdwara nearby can still live as Sikhs.
  • Another view: the gurdwara and daily life support each other: what Sikhs learn and practise there shapes the rest of the week.
  • Judge it by: Is "Sikh life" mainly worship, or the whole of life? What did the Gurus stress: place, people, or practice?
Mission 1Worked answer

Two features, developed

Question: Explain two features of a gurdwara and why they are important to Sikhs.

  • Feature 1: the takht, under a chanani. Development: the Guru Granth Sahib is placed higher than anyone and under a canopy, because Sikhs honour it as their living Guru, like a sovereign.
  • Feature 2: the langar hall. Development: everyone eats the same free meal sitting in rows, which puts into practice the Sikh belief that all people are equal before God.
Mission check

?A Sikh family moves to a remote area with no gurdwara nearby. They set aside a clean room, install the Guru Granth Sahib with a canopy and cloths, and invite neighbours to pray and eat together on Sundays. Most Sikhs would say:

A gurdwara is the door of the Guru: where the Guru Granth Sahib is honoured, the sangat gathers and everyone is fed.

Mission 2

Mission 2: Can repeating one word, again and again, change who you are?

Make a guess: Can repeating one word, again and again, change who you are?

Mission 2

What nam japna means

  • Nam: God's Name, meaning God's nature and presence in everything, not just a word.
  • Japna: to repeat, recite and meditate on.
  • Nam japna (meditating on God's Name) is the first of the three things Guru Nanak taught every Sikh to do:
  • Nam japna (remember God), kirat karni (earn an honest living), vand chhakna (share with others).
  • Your spec calls this "meditating on the name of God".
Mission 2

Ways of nam japna

  • Repeating "Waheguru" ("Wonderful Lord"), the name most Sikhs use for God, silently or aloud, often in rhythm with the breath.
  • Some Sikhs use a mala (string of prayer beads) to keep focus; many do not.
  • Reciting and singing Gurbani: the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Amrit vela: the early hours before dawn, which Sikhs see as the best time.
  • In the gurdwara: the sangat sings kirtan and chants "Waheguru" together in simran sessions.
  • In daily life: remembering God while working, travelling or cooking, not only at set times.
Mission 2

Why it matters

  • Sikhs believe the mind is pulled away from God by haumai (ego) and the five thieves (lust, anger, greed, attachment, pride).
  • Nam japna turns the mind back to God, making a person gurmukh (God-centred) rather than manmukh (self-centred).
  • It brings inner peace and the courage to face hardship (chardi kala, rising spirits).
  • Sikhs believe it prepares the soul for mukti (liberation), which comes by God's grace (nadar).
  • It is not magic: the aim is a changed heart, shown in honest work and sharing.
Quick check
?Which statement best explains why nam japna matters to Sikhs?
Mission 2Read the source

Guru Granth Sahib 305

Guru Granth Sahib 305 (Guru Ram Das, paraphrase): one who calls himself a Sikh of the True Guru should rise early and meditate on the Lord's Name. He should make the effort in the early hours, bathe in the pool of nectar, and repeat the Name as the Guru teaches. Through the day he sings the Guru's hymns, and remembers God with every breath and every bite of food.

Q1 When should a Sikh begin to pray?

Show answer

Early in the morning, before dawn.

Q2 Does prayer stop when the morning prayers end?

Show answer

No: God is remembered with every breath, all day.

Mission 2

Prayer at home: Nitnem

  • Nitnem: the daily set prayers, read from a gutka (prayer book), after bathing, with head covered.
  • Morning (amrit vela): Japji Sahib (Guru Nanak), Jaap Sahib and Tav-Prasad Savaiye (Guru Gobind Singh). Many add Chaupai Sahib and Anand Sahib.
  • Evening: Rehras Sahib.
  • Night, before sleep: Kirtan Sohila.
  • Some families also gather to read, sing kirtan, or take a hukamnama if the Guru Granth Sahib is kept at home.
  • Role: it shapes the day around God, from waking to sleeping, and teaches children the prayers.
Mission 2

Different prayers, different purposes

  • Nitnem: praise and remembrance at fixed times every day.
  • Ardas: a standing prayer of petition and thanks, said at the end of worship and before or after any important task (a journey, an exam, a meal).
  • Simran: personal, silent remembrance of God's Name at any time.
  • Optional banis: e.g. Sukhmani Sahib (Guru Arjan), read for peace of mind.
  • Why have different prayers? Each meets a need: to praise, to ask, to thank, to stay calm, to remember God through the whole day.
Mission 2

Kirtan and Ardas in the gurdwara

  • Kirtan: singing Gurbani to music (harmonium, tabla), led by ragis. Guru Nanak sang his hymns with Bhai Mardana.
  • Sikhs believe singing and hearing Gurbani is itself nam japna: the mind is absorbed in the Guru's word.
  • Ardas: the sangat stands facing the Guru Granth Sahib, hands joined.
  • It remembers God, the Ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs who gave their lives for their faith.
  • It ends with a prayer for all: "by your will, may all be blessed" (sarbat da bhala).
Quick check
?Which description fits the Ardas?
Mission 2Evaluate

"Nam japna is the most important Sikh practice."

  • Reasons for: it is the first of Guru Nanak's three teachings; GGS 305 makes remembering God the mark of a true Sikh; it overcomes haumai and leads towards mukti.
  • Reasons against: Guru Nanak taught three duties together: nam japna without honest work and sharing would be empty. Sewa and langar express faith in action. For Khalsa Sikhs, keeping Amrit and the Five Ks is also central.
  • Another view: the practices are one: honest work and sewa done while remembering God are nam japna in daily life.
  • Judge it by: Can inner devotion and outward action be separated? What did the Gurus say makes someone a Sikh?
Mission check

?A Sikh nurse cannot get to the gurdwara during a run of night shifts. Between patients she silently repeats "Waheguru", and reads Kirtan Sohila on her break before sleeping. Which Sikh teaching does her practice show best?

Nam japna is not confined to a building or an hour: Sikhs aim to remember God with every breath.

Mission 3

Mission 3: Why would people read a 1,430-page book aloud for two days without a single pause?

Make a guess: Why would people read a 1,430-page book aloud for two days without a single pause?

Mission 3

An unbroken reading

  • Akhand Path: a continuous, unbroken (akhand) reading (path) of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, from the first page to the last.
  • All 1,430 angs, read aloud, without stopping: it takes about 48 hours.
  • A team of trained readers (pathis) takes turns, often about two hours each.
  • At each change, the new reader joins mid-line so that not a word is missed.
  • Your spec spells it Akand Path.
Mission 3

Beginning and end

  • Beginning: karah prashad is prepared; six verses of Anand Sahib are sung; Ardas is said; a hukamnama is taken; the reading starts.
  • During: the sangat comes and goes to listen at all hours; langar is served throughout.
  • End (bhog): the final pages are read; Anand Sahib is sung; Ardas is said; a hukamnama is taken; karah prashad and langar are shared.
  • Often kirtan is sung at the bhog, and the family who arranged the path thank the sangat.
Quick check
?During an Akhand Path, a reader's two-hour turn ends in the middle of a hymn. What happens?
Mission 3

Where did it come from?

  • Its exact origin is not recorded.
  • Many Sikhs link it to the 18th century, when Sikhs were persecuted and often scattered. Groups would read the whole scripture in one continuous sitting, so that the complete Guru's word could be heard when they could gather.
  • Some traditions trace continuous readings back to the time of Guru Gobind Singh.
  • Since then it has become part of Sikh life worldwide: in gurdwaras every week and in homes.
Mission 3

When is an Akhand Path held?

  • Joy: a birth, a wedding, moving into a new home, opening a business, success in exams.
  • Sorrow or hardship: after a death, during illness, at a time of trouble.
  • Festivals and gurpurbs: timed so that the bhog falls on the morning of the festival day.
  • Anniversaries: e.g. of a family member's death.
  • It may be held in a gurdwara or, if a clean, separate room is ready, at home.
Mission 3

Why it matters

  • For the community: the sangat hears the whole of the Guru's word together; many share the sewa (reading, listening, cooking langar, giving money); it unites families and gurdwaras at key moments.
  • For the individual: a way to thank God in joy and find comfort in sorrow; hearing Gurbani steadies the mind (nam japna); some Sikhs train to read, a deep act of devotion.
  • How Sikhs take part: reading a turn, listening at any hour (even through the night), cooking or serving langar, donating, attending the bhog.
Mission 3Diversity

Akhand Path and other complete readings

  • Sahaj Path (easy reading): a complete reading at a slower pace, over days, weeks or months, at home or in the gurdwara, with time to understand.
  • Saptahik Path: a complete reading spread over seven days.
  • Some Sikhs see the Akhand Path as a powerful offering of the whole community.
  • Others worry that paying readers who read with no one listening, or holding one only for good luck, turns it into ritual: the Rahit Maryada warns against both.
  • Many say what matters is listening and living by the words, whichever kind of reading is chosen.
Quick check
?A family plans an Akhand Path to thank God for a new baby. Which practice would the Rahit Maryada say is wrong?
Mission 3Evaluate

"An Akhand Path is the best way for Sikhs to mark an important event."

  • Reasons for: the whole Guru's word is heard; the sangat shares the sewa; it fits joy and sorrow alike; it ends with Ardas, hukamnama and langar, bringing together worship, guidance and equality.
  • Reasons against: a Sahaj Path gives more time to understand the words; nam japna and sewa can mark events every day; if no one listens, it becomes ritual; it costs time and money not every family has.
  • Another view: the occasion matters less than the attitude: any act that turns the family to the Guru marks the event well.
  • Judge it by: Is hearing every word or understanding the words more important? Who takes part? Does it change how people live afterwards?
Mission check

?A British Sikh family has lost their grandfather. They arrange for a Sahaj Path at home over three weeks instead of an Akhand Path, reading a little each evening together. How would most Sikhs view this?

An Akhand Path is the whole Guru speaking, without a break, at the moments that matter: and someone must be listening.

Mission 4

Mission 4: How can a Sikh baby's name come from a page of scripture opened at random?

Make a guess: How can a Sikh baby's name come from a page of scripture opened at random?

Mission 4

Welcoming a baby

  • Sikhs see a child as a gift from God, born by God's will (hukam).
  • In many families, soon after birth, the Mool Mantar (the opening words of the Guru Granth Sahib) or "Waheguru" (Wonderful Lord) is whispered in the baby's ear: the first words the child hears are about God.
  • Some families give a drop of sweetened water (amrit), stirred with a kirpan, or of honey.
  • The family visits the gurdwara for the naming once the mother is well. There is no fixed day.
  • The Sikh code rejects the idea that birth makes a home "impure" for a set number of days.
Mission 4

Naam Karan, step by step

  • Naam Karan: "naming ceremony", in the gurdwara with the sangat (congregation).
  • The family brings karah prashad (sweet blessed food) and often a rumala (cloth) to cover the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Hymns of joy and thanks are sung.
  • The Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random and a hymn is read: the hukamnama, the Guru's "order" or guidance for that moment.
  • The first letter of the first word of the hymn is announced. A name is chosen beginning with that letter.
  • The name is announced and the sangat agrees, often with the shout "Jo bole so nihal, Sat Sri Akal".
  • Singh is added for a boy, Kaur for a girl.
  • Closing: six verses of Anand Sahib, Ardas (prayer) giving thanks, karah prashad shared; often langar.
Mission 4Read the source

The Sikh code of conduct

The Sikh Rahit Maryada (the Sikh code of conduct, approved by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee in 1945), on birth and naming (paraphrase):

  • Go to the gurdwara when the mother is able to move about and bathe; the number of days does not matter.
  • Take the hukam by opening the Guru Granth Sahib. The granthi proposes a name beginning with the first letter of the hymn; it is announced once the sangat accepts it.
  • Add Singh to a boy's name and Kaur to a girl's.
  • Do not hold that birth causes ritual pollution: birth and death happen by God's will.

Q1 Who has the final say in choosing the letter?

Show answer

The Guru Granth Sahib, through the hukam.

Q2 What belief about birth does the code reject?

Show answer

That it makes a family impure for a set number of days.

Quick check
?In the Naam Karan ceremony, what is the hukamnama?
Mission 4

What the ceremony means

  • Guided by the Guru: the name comes from the Guru's word, so from the start the child's life is placed under the Guru's guidance.
  • Thanks to God: the child is God's gift, not something the family made alone.
  • Belonging: the sangat welcomes the child into the Sikh community.
  • Equality: the same ceremony for girls and boys; most Sikh names (e.g. Harpreet, Jaspreet) are used for both.
  • No superstition: no horoscopes, no lucky days, no "impure" period.
  • Many families celebrate with sweets and gifts for relatives and friends.
Mission 4

Singh and Kaur: where they come from

  • At Vaisakhi 1699, Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa (the community of initiated Sikhs).
  • He gave the men the name Singh ("lion") and the women Kaur (usually translated "princess").
  • In India, family surnames often showed caste. Using Singh or Kaur instead hides caste: all are equal members of one family, the Guru's.
  • Lion: courage to stand for truth and protect the weak.
  • Princess: dignity and royalty for every woman, whatever her birth.
  • A Kaur keeps her name for life; she does not have to take her husband's name.
Quick check
?Why did Guru Gobind Singh give Sikhs the names Singh and Kaur?
Mission 4Diversity

Singh, Kaur and naming today

  • Most Sikhs receive Singh or Kaur at the naming ceremony.
  • Use varies in Britain: some use Singh or Kaur as their surname; many add a family name (e.g. Sandhu, Gill), with Singh or Kaur as a middle name.
  • Some Sikhs argue that family names bring caste back in, against the Guru's aim. Others say a family name is practical for official forms and shows family heritage, not caste pride.
  • Some Sikh women in Britain take a husband's surname; others keep Kaur, as the Rahit Maryada expects.
  • Khalsa (amritdhari) families tend to follow the Rahit Maryada closely: hukam letter, no superstition.
  • Some non-Khalsa families add Punjabi customs alongside, such as celebrating a first Lohri (winter festival) for a new baby; many now hold it for daughters as well as sons.
  • At Amrit Sanskar (a later mission), anyone without Singh or Kaur takes the name.
Mission 4Evaluate

"Singh and Kaur still matter for Sikh identity today."

  • Reasons for: they come from Guru Gobind Singh and mark belonging to the Khalsa family; they reject caste; Kaur gives women independent identity; a name is a daily reminder of courage and dignity.
  • Reasons against: many Sikhs now use family names as surnames, so Singh and Kaur often appear only as middle names; identity is shown more by belief and action (Nam Japna, sewa) than by a name; "Singh" is also used by some non-Sikhs in India, so it does not always identify a Sikh.
  • Judge it by: What did the Guru intend? Do names change how people treat each other? Is identity mainly inner or outward?
Mission 4Worked answer

Practice, meaning, source

Question: Explain two ways the naming ceremony is significant for Sikhs.

  • Point 1: The name comes from the hukamnama. Development: the first letter of a hymn from the Guru Granth Sahib guides the name, so the child's life begins under the Guru's guidance (Rahit Maryada, birth and naming).
  • Point 2: Singh or Kaur is added. Development: this shows the child is an equal member of the Guru's family with no caste, as Guru Gobind Singh intended in 1699.
Mission check

?At a naming ceremony, the hukamnama begins with a word starting "J". The baby's grandmother had hoped to name the girl Simran, after her own mother. What would a family following the Rahit Maryada most likely do?

A Sikh name joins guidance from the Guru's word with the equality of the Guru's family.

Mission 5

Mission 5: If Sikhs believe God is everywhere, why do so many travel to one temple in Amritsar?

Make a guess: If Sikhs believe God is everywhere, why do so many travel to one temple in Amritsar?

Mission 5

Amritsar: the pool of nectar

  • Amritsar (Punjab, India) means "pool of nectar".
  • Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, began the city in the 1570s and had a large pool (sarovar) dug.
  • Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, completed the pool and built a gurdwara in the middle of it.
  • Traders and craftworkers settled; the city grew into a centre of both faith and business.
  • Today Amritsar is called the spiritual centre of Sikhism: the most visited Sikh place of pilgrimage.
Mission 5

Building the Harmandir Sahib

  • Harmandir Sahib: "temple of God". Often called the Golden Temple; also Darbar Sahib.
  • Your spec spells it Harmander Sahib.
  • Building began in 1588. Sikh tradition says the Muslim Sufi saint Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone: a sign of openness.
  • In 1604 Guru Arjan installed the newly compiled Adi Granth (the scripture, later the Guru Granth Sahib) inside; Baba Buddha became its first reader (granthi).
  • Destroyed in the 1700s by Afghan invaders and rebuilt by the Sikhs.
  • Maharaja Ranjit Singh covered the upper storeys in gold in the early 1800s: hence "Golden Temple".
Mission 5

Features and their meaning

  • Four doors, one on each side: open to people of every direction, caste and religion.
  • Built lower than the land around it: visitors step down to enter, a lesson in humility.
  • Stands in the sarovar, reached by a causeway from a gateway (Darshani Deori).
  • A marble walkway (parikrama) runs round the pool.
  • Inside: the Guru Granth Sahib, and kirtan (hymns from it) sung from early morning to late at night.
  • Facing the causeway: the Akal Takht. Nearby: the huge langar hall.
Quick check
?Visitors step down into the Harmandir Sahib, and it has doors on all four sides. What do most Sikhs say these two features teach?
Mission 5

A pilgrim's day

  • Before dawn: the Guru Granth Sahib is carried in a palanquin (palki) from the Akal Takht and opened in the Harmandir Sahib (prakash).
  • Pilgrims cover their heads, remove shoes and wash their feet.
  • Many bathe (ishnan) in the sarovar, then walk the parikrama clockwise.
  • They queue to bow (matha tekna) before the Guru Granth Sahib and listen to kirtan.
  • They receive karah prashad.
  • They do sewa (selfless service): cleaning the walkway, minding shoes, washing dishes.
  • Langar: volunteers serve a free vegetarian meal to a huge number of people every day, all sitting on the floor in rows (pangat), whatever their wealth, caste or religion.
  • At night: the Guru Granth Sahib is carried back to the Akal Takht to rest (sukhasan).
Mission 5Diversity

Should Sikhs go on pilgrimage?

  • Pilgrimage is not compulsory in Sikhism. Guru Nanak criticised the belief that bathing at holy places washes away sin.
  • Reasons many Sikhs visit: to see where the Gurus lived and taught; to feel the history; to join a huge sangat; to do sewa; to renew faith.
  • Other historical gurdwaras: Nankana Sahib (Guru Nanak's birthplace, Pakistan); Kartarpur (where he died); Anandpur Sahib (where the Khalsa began); the five takhts.
  • Some Sikhs stress the inner journey: God is everywhere; the local gurdwara and daily Nam Japna matter more than travel.
  • Some believe bathing in the sarovar brings healing; others call this superstition the Gurus rejected.
  • For Sikhs in Britain, a visit can be a link with family roots in Punjab.
Quick check
?Which statement best describes Sikh teaching about pilgrimage?
Mission 5Evaluate

"Every Sikh should visit the Harmandir Sahib."

  • Reasons for: it is the place the Gurus built and the scripture was first installed; the sangat, kirtan and langar there show Sikh values on a vast scale; it strengthens identity, especially for Sikhs far from Punjab.
  • Reasons against: the Gurus taught that God is everywhere and that outward pilgrimage brings "a little merit"; cost and travel are not possible for all; daily Nam Japna and sewa at the local gurdwara matter more.
  • Another view: a visit is a gift, not a duty: worthwhile if it deepens inner devotion.
  • Judge it by: What did the Gurus teach about outward ritual? Does the experience change how a person lives? Is "should" a duty or an encouragement?
Mission check

?A Sikh grandmother in Glasgow is too ill to travel to Amritsar and is sad she will never see the Harmandir Sahib. What response would most Sikhs give her, based on the Gurus' teaching?

Amritsar is the heart of Sikh history and community, but the Gurus taught that the deepest pilgrimage is inward.

Mission 6

Mission 6: Why did a Guru ask a huge crowd which of them would give him their head?

Make a guess: Why did a Guru ask a huge crowd which of them would give him their head?

Mission 6

Before 1699: a harvest festival

  • Vaisakhi falls in April (usually 13 or 14 April). In Punjab it marks the spring harvest and the solar new year.
  • Guru Amar Das (3rd Guru) asked Sikhs to gather at Goindwal at Vaisakhi, to meet the Guru and each other.
  • So it was already a Sikh gathering day before 1699.
  • For Sikhs today, its main meaning comes from what happened at Anandpur in 1699.
Mission 6

Anandpur, 1699: the call

  • Guru Gobind Singh called Sikhs to Anandpur for Vaisakhi. Sikhs had suffered persecution; his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, had been executed (1675).
  • Sikh accounts tell the story like this. Before the huge gathering he drew his sword and asked: who will give his head for the Guru?
  • After a silence, one man stood. The Guru took him into a tent and came out with a bloodied sword.
  • He asked again, and again: five men in all came forward.
  • Then the Guru brought all five out, alive, dressed alike in new clothes.
  • Sikhs call them the panj pyare (the five beloved ones).
Mission 6

The panj pyare

  • Bhai Daya Singh, Bhai Dharam Singh, Bhai Himmat Singh, Bhai Mohkam Singh, Bhai Sahib Singh.
  • In traditional accounts they came from different regions of India (from Lahore in the north to Bidar in the south).
  • They came from different castes: a trader, a farmer, a water-carrier, a tailor and a barber.
  • Their courage and devotion are remembered in every Ardas.
  • Today five respected amritdhari Sikhs act as panj pyare: they lead Amrit ceremonies and processions.
Mission 6

Amrit and the birth of the Khalsa

  • The Guru stirred water in an iron bowl with a khanda (double-edged sword) while reciting prayers.
  • Sugar sweets were added: Khalsa courage should come with sweetness and kindness.
  • The five drank amrit from the one bowl: a break with caste rules.
  • Sikh accounts say the Guru then asked the five to give amrit to him: Guru and Khalsa stand as equals.
  • Men took the name Singh (lion), women Kaur (princess).
  • They became the Khalsa ("pure", belonging to God), keeping the Five Ks and a strict code of life.
Quick check
?Why is it important to Sikhs that Guru Gobind Singh asked the panj pyare to give amrit to him after he had given it to them?
Mission 6

Why Vaisakhi matters

  • It celebrates the birth of the Khalsa and a Sikh identity that can be seen (the Five Ks, the turban).
  • Commitment: the panj pyare show complete dedication to God and the Guru.
  • Equality: different castes drank from one bowl and shared one name.
  • Courage: standing up for faith and for others' freedom, as Guru Tegh Bahadur had done.
  • Renewal: many Sikhs choose Vaisakhi to take amrit themselves, or to renew their commitment.
Mission 6

How Sikhs celebrate

  • Akhand Path ending on Vaisakhi morning; kirtan and talks on the events of 1699; Ardas; karah prashad; langar.
  • Nishan Sahib: the flagpole is taken down and washed, and dressed with a new cloth and flag.
  • Amrit ceremonies: led by five Khalsa Sikhs acting as panj pyare.
  • Nagar kirtan ("town singing"): a street procession led by five Sikhs as panj pyare, with the Guru Granth Sahib on a decorated float, kirtan, and displays of gatka (Sikh martial art).
  • Along the route, Sikhs serve free food and drink to everyone, including passers-by.
  • Gurdwaras are decorated; families wear new clothes and visit relatives.
Quick check
?At a Vaisakhi nagar kirtan, five Sikhs in matching robes walk at the front, ahead of the float carrying the Guru Granth Sahib. Whom do they represent?
Mission 6Diversity

India and Britain

  • In Punjab, India: a public holiday; harvest fairs, music and bhangra; very large gatherings at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, at Anandpur Sahib, and at Damdama Sahib (Talwandi Sabo).
  • In Britain: usually celebrated at the nearest weekend, since 13/14 April is often a working or school day.
  • British cities with large Sikh communities hold big nagar kirtans; some city councils host public Vaisakhi events.
  • In Britain the religious meaning (the Khalsa) is often more to the fore; the harvest side matters less away from Punjab's farms.
  • In Britain, Vaisakhi is also a chance to explain Sikhism to neighbours of other faiths.
Mission 6Diversity

Different understandings

  • Amritdhari Sikhs (initiated) often see Vaisakhi as a day of commitment: renewing their vows, or helping others take amrit.
  • Sahajdhari Sikhs (not initiated) celebrate fully too, while some feel not yet ready to take amrit.
  • Festival or remembrance? Some see Vaisakhi as a gurpurb-like celebration of the Khalsa's birth; others stress the harvest and new-year festival shared with Punjabi neighbours of all faiths.
  • Some Sikhs worry that music, fairs and parties overshadow the religious meaning; others say joy and community are part of the festival.
Mission 6Evaluate

"Vaisakhi is the most important Sikh festival."

  • Reasons for: it marks the birth of the Khalsa, which shapes Sikh identity today; many take amrit then; it is the largest public Sikh celebration in Britain.
  • Reasons against: Guru Nanak's birthday celebrates the founder of the faith; martyrdom days (Guru Arjan, Guru Tegh Bahadur) and Bandi Chhor Divas carry deep meaning; Sikhs believe no single day matters more than daily nam japna and sewa.
  • Another view: Sikhs weigh this differently: some give Guru Nanak's gurpurb the greater weight; many amritdhari Sikhs feel Vaisakhi most strongly.
  • Judge it by: What is being remembered? Which festival most shapes Sikh life afterwards? Are festivals more important than daily practice?
Mission check

?A British Sikh teenager decides to take amrit at Vaisakhi. Her non-Sikh friend asks why she chose that day. Which answer would a Sikh give?

At Vaisakhi, Sikhs remember five people of different castes who offered everything, and the Khalsa that began with them.

Mission 7

Mission 7: Why do Sikhs light up the Golden Temple to remember a Guru walking out of prison?

Make a guess: Why do Sikhs light up the Golden Temple to remember a Guru walking out of prison?

Mission 7

Gurpurbs and melas

  • Gurpurb: "the Guru's day". Mostly the birth or death anniversary of one of the Gurus.
  • The death of a Guru killed for the faith is a martyrdom (shaheedi) day.
  • Mela: a "fair" or gathering. Examples: Vaisakhi, Divali, Hola Mohalla (a festival of martial skills begun by Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur).
  • Many melas fall on dates also kept by Hindus. Guru Amar Das asked Sikhs to gather around the Guru at Vaisakhi and Divali, giving those days a Sikh meaning.
  • Common practices: an akhand path (a continuous 48-hour reading of the Guru Granth Sahib) ending on the day, kirtan (hymn-singing), decorations, karah prashad (blessed sweet food) and langar (free shared meal).
  • Spec spelling: Divali.
Mission 7

Bandi Chhor: the Guru who freed prisoners

  • Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, was held in Gwalior Fort by the Mughal emperor Jahangir (early 1600s).
  • Jahangir agreed to free him. The Guru refused to go unless 52 Hindu princes (rajas) held there were freed too.
  • Jahangir said: only those who can hold on to your cloak may leave.
  • The Guru had a cloak made with 52 tassels. Each prince held one and walked out with him.
  • He reached Amritsar at Divali time; the Harmandir Sahib was lit with lamps to welcome him.
  • He became known as Bandi Chhor: "the one who frees prisoners". Bandi Chhor Divas: "day of release".
Quick check
?Why is Guru Hargobind called "Bandi Chhor"?
Mission 7

Divali for Sikhs

  • Same time of year as the Hindu Divali (October or November), but a different story.
  • Hindus remember, for example, Rama's return to Ayodhya; Sikhs remember Guru Hargobind's release.
  • At the Harmandir Sahib: the buildings and pool are lit with lamps; fireworks over Amritsar.
  • In gurdwaras: kirtan, Ardas (the community prayer), karah prashad, langar.
  • At home: lamps or candles, sweets and gifts with family and friends.
  • Many Sikhs also remember Bhai Mani Singh, a Sikh scholar executed in Lahore in the 1730s after a dispute over a Divali gathering at Amritsar.
  • Some Sikhs prefer the name Bandi Chhor Divas, to show the Sikh meaning; others say Divali and share the season with Hindu neighbours.
Mission 7

Guru Nanak's birthday

  • Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan.
  • Most Sikhs celebrate at the full moon of the month of Kartik (usually November).
  • An akhand path ends on the morning of the gurpurb.
  • Nagar kirtan: a street procession singing hymns. The Guru Granth Sahib is carried on a decorated float, led by five Sikhs (panj pyare) carrying the Nishan Sahib (Sikh flag).
  • Gurdwaras are lit up; there are talks on the Guru's life, kirtan through the night and langar for everyone.
  • Many pilgrims travel to Nankana Sahib for the day.
  • Meaning: thanks for the Guru who first taught the Sikh path: one God, equality, honest work, sharing.
Mission 7

Martyrdoms: Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur

  • Guru Arjan (fifth Guru) compiled the Adi Granth and built the Harmandir Sahib.
  • In 1606 he was tortured and killed in Lahore on the orders of Jahangir: Sikhs remember him seated on a burning-hot iron plate.
  • His martyrdom day falls in early summer. Sikhs set up chhabeel stalls giving cold sweet drinks to anyone passing: kindness answers cruelty.
  • Guru Tegh Bahadur (ninth Guru) was beheaded in Delhi in 1675 on the orders of the emperor Aurangzeb.
  • He had stood up for Hindu Pandits from Kashmir who were being forced to convert: he died defending other people's freedom of religion.
  • Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Delhi marks the place. His day falls in late November or December.
  • Martyrdom days are kept more quietly: kirtan, an akhand path, talks on the Guru's sacrifice, langar.
Mission 7Read the source

"He gave his head"

Guru Gobind Singh (Guru Tegh Bahadur's son) wrote about his father in the Bachittar Natak (paraphrase):

  • He protected the forehead mark and sacred thread of the Hindus (their right to their own religion).
  • He gave his head, but did not give up his faith; he gave his life, but not his resolve.

Q1 Whose religious freedom did Guru Tegh Bahadur die for?

Show answer

Hindus': he defended the right of others to their own faith.

Q2 What, according to the poem, did he refuse to give up?

Show answer

His faith and resolve.

Quick check
?Which statement about the martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur is correct?
Mission 7Diversity

Same festival, different places and views

  • In India (Punjab): Guru Nanak's birthday is a public holiday; huge crowds at historic gurdwaras; pilgrimages to Nankana Sahib and Amritsar.
  • In Britain: celebrations often move to the nearest weekend, because of school and work.
  • British nagar kirtans go through town streets (e.g. Southall, Birmingham, Leicester), with police and council planning.
  • British gurdwaras often open langar to neighbours and invite schools: a chance to share Sikh values and teach children their heritage.
  • Different communities in Britain, such as Ramgarhia and Bhatra gurdwaras, may run their own programmes on different days.
  • Dates differ too: some Sikhs follow the Nanakshahi calendar (fixed dates), others the traditional lunar dates.
Quick check
?A gurdwara in Britain holds an akhand path and a nagar kirtan, led by five Sikhs carrying the Nishan Sahib, on the Sunday nearest the full moon of Kartik. Which gurpurb is it most likely to be?
Mission 7Evaluate

"Festivals are the most important part of Sikh life."

  • Reasons for: festivals keep the Gurus' stories alive for the next generation; they gather the sangat (community); nagar kirtans and langar show Sikh values in public; martyrdoms inspire courage and justice.
  • Reasons against: the Gurus stressed daily devotion: Nam Japna (meditating on God's name), honest work and sharing; a festival once a year cannot replace this. Some see too much spending and fireworks. Guru Nanak criticised empty ritual.
  • Another view: festivals and daily life support each other: the festival renews the commitment that daily life keeps.
  • Judge it by: What did the Gurus themselves teach about ritual? What keeps faith strong in a minority community such as Britain? Is "important" about frequency or about impact?
Mission 7Worked answer

Belief, story, meaning

Question: Explain two reasons why Divali is important to Sikhs.

  • Reason 1: It remembers Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior Fort. Development: he would not leave without the 52 princes, so Sikhs see in it a duty to stand up for other people's freedom, not only their own.
  • Reason 2: It brings the sangat together at the gurdwara. Development: lamps, kirtan, karah prashad and langar renew faith together and pass the story on to children, which matters for Sikhs living as a minority in Britain.
Mission check

?At Bandi Chhor Divas, a gurdwara in Leeds collects letters of support for people around the world who are imprisoned for their beliefs. Which part of the Sikh story does this most directly reflect?

Sikh festivals turn history into action: remembering the Gurus means standing for freedom, justice and the sangat today.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Gurdwara = door of the Guru: Nishan Sahib and the open-door idea outside; takht, palki, chanani, chaur and rumalas inside; sach khand and langar hall.
  • Bhatra and Ramgarhia gurdwaras serve as places of worship and as community centres for particular British Sikh communities.

Mission 2

  • Nam japna (meditating on God's Name) is the first of Guru Nanak's three duties; repeating "Waheguru", Gurbani and kirtan turn the mind from ego to God.
  • Prayer at home: Nitnem (morning, evening, night), Ardas, simran; GGS 305 calls a Sikh to rise early and remember God all day.

Mission 3

  • Akhand Path: unbroken reading of all 1,430 angs, about 48 hours, by relays of readers; starts and ends (bhog) with Anand Sahib, Ardas, hukamnama and karah prashad.
  • Held for births, weddings, deaths and gurpurbs; Sahaj Path is a slower complete reading.

Mission 4

  • Naam Karan: in the gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random; the first letter of the hukamnama guides the name.
  • Singh ("lion") and Kaur ("princess"), given since 1699, show equality and reject caste.
  • How Sikhs use Singh, Kaur and family names today varies, and is debated.

Mission 5

  • Guru Ram Das began Amritsar; Guru Arjan built the Harmandir Sahib (1588–1604) and installed the scripture there.
  • Four doors (open to all) and a lower level (humility); pilgrims bathe, walk the parikrama, hear kirtan, do sewa and eat langar.

Mission 6

  • Vaisakhi: a Punjabi harvest festival, a Sikh gathering since Guru Amar Das, and the birth of the Khalsa at Anandpur in 1699.
  • Panj pyare, amrit from one iron bowl, Singh and Kaur: commitment, courage and equality.
  • Celebrated with Akhand Path, a new Nishan Sahib, amrit ceremonies and nagar kirtan; in Britain at weekends, with a stronger religious focus.

Mission 7

  • Gurpurbs mark the Gurus' births and martyrdoms; melas such as Divali are gatherings given a Sikh meaning.
  • Divali / Bandi Chhor Divas remembers Guru Hargobind freeing himself and 52 princes; Guru Nanak's birthday is marked with an akhand path and nagar kirtan.
  • Guru Arjan (1606) and Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675) are remembered as martyrs for truth and freedom of religion.
